cards.headline: Energy shrinks as it moves up a food chain
lines: Plants capture sunlight; plant-eaters eat plants; predators eat plant-eaters.
Only about 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next.
That's why there are far fewer lions than zebras.

visual.caption: Energy passed up each level (≈ 10% rule)

cards.source: Lindeman (1942), 'The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology', Ecology; Campbell Biology.

cards.headline: The longest migration of any animal
lines: Arctic terns fly from Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back every year.
Tracked birds averaged about 70,000 km per round trip.
Over a lifetime, that's like flying to the Moon and back about three times.

visual.caption: an Arctic tern's yearly round trip

cards.source: Egevang et al. (2010), 'Tracking of Arctic Terns', PNAS.

cards.headline: The ocean makes much of our oxygen
lines: Microscopic drifting algae and bacteria called phytoplankton photosynthesise, just like land plants.
They account for roughly half of all photosynthesis on Earth.
Their growth depends on sunlight, nutrients and water temperature.

visual.caption: of Earth's photosynthesis happens at sea

cards.source: Field et al. (1998), 'Primary Production of the Biosphere', Science; NOAA Ocean Service.

cards.headline: The water cycle
lines: The Sun evaporates water from oceans, lakes and leaves.
The vapour cools into clouds and falls as rain or snow.
It flows back to the sea through rivers and the ground — and starts again.
cards.source: US Geological Survey, Water Science School: 'The Water Cycle'.

cards.headline: Keystone species
lines: Some species have an effect far larger than their numbers suggest.
Robert Paine removed a predatory starfish from a shoreline: mussels took over and diversity crashed.
Sea otters protect kelp forests by eating the urchins that graze them.
cards.source: Paine (1966, 1969), American Naturalist; Estes & Palmisano (1974), Science.

cards.question: Which is the heaviest animal known to have lived?
cards.why: Blue whales reach about 30 m and well over 100 tonnes — heavier than any known dinosaur.
cards.source: NOAA Fisheries, blue whale species profile.

cards.question: Why are bees so important to farming?
cards.why: Carrying pollen between flowers lets many fruits, nuts and vegetables form.
cards.source: Klein et al. (2007), 'Importance of Pollinators in Changing Landscapes for World Crops', Proc R Soc B.

cards.question: Which tiny animal survived exposure to open space on a satellite in 2007?
cards.why: Dried-out tardigrades ('water bears') survived the vacuum of space on the FOTON-M3 mission.
cards.source: Jönsson et al. (2008), 'Tardigrades Survive Exposure to Space in Low Earth Orbit', Current Biology.

cards.question: Roughly what share of energy passes from one level of a food chain to the next?
cards.why: Most energy is used for living or lost as heat, so only around a tenth moves up.
cards.source: Campbell Biology, energy flow in ecosystems.

cards.question: How many hearts does an octopus have?
cards.why: Two pump blood through the gills, and one pumps it around the rest of the body.
cards.source: Wells, 'Octopus: Physiology and Behaviour of an Advanced Invertebrate' (1978).

cards.headline: Some living trees are over 4,500 years old
cards.text: Great Basin bristlecone pines in California's White Mountains include individuals dated by tree rings at more than 4,800 years.
cards.source: Schulman (1958), National Geographic; US Forest Service, Ancient Bristlecone Pine Forest.

cards.headline: One of the largest living things is a fungus
cards.text: A honey fungus (Armillaria) in Oregon's Blue Mountains spreads underground over roughly 9 square kilometres.
cards.source: Ferguson et al. (2003), Canadian Journal of Forest Research; US Forest Service.

cards.headline: Sharks are older than trees
cards.text: Shark fossils go back more than 400 million years. The first trees appeared around 385 million years ago.
cards.source: Benton, 'Vertebrate Palaeontology'; Stein et al. (2007), Nature (early forests).

cards.headline: Hummingbirds can fly backwards
cards.text: Their wings rotate at the shoulder and trace a figure-eight, letting them hover and reverse — something almost no other bird can do.
cards.source: Warrick, Tobalske & Powers (2005), 'Aerodynamics of the Hovering Hummingbird', Nature.

steps.headline: 1 · Light in
lines: Chlorophyll in leaf cells absorbs mostly red and blue light.
It reflects green — which is why leaves look green.

steps.headline: 2 · Water up, CO₂ in
lines: Roots draw water up the stem.
Tiny pores called stomata let carbon dioxide in.

steps.headline: 3 · Sugar made
lines: Using the light's energy, the plant splits water and builds glucose from CO₂.
Oxygen is released as a by-product.

steps.headline: 4 · Stored and used
lines: Glucose fuels the plant and is stored as starch or built into cellulose.
Nearly every food chain on land starts here.

cards.headline: Nature: the takeaways
points: Only about 10% of energy moves up a food chain.
Ocean phytoplankton do about half of Earth's photosynthesis.
Water cycles: evaporate, condense, fall, collect.
Arctic terns fly about 70,000 km a year.
